title: Global Budgets for Hospitals: Maryland & Beyond
summary: How global hospital budgets set annual spending targets that decouple hospital revenue from volume — the Maryland Model, Vermont, and the evidence on cost and quality.

objectives.text: Explain what a global budget is and how it differs from capitation or fee-for-service
Describe Maryland's all-payer hospital global budget model and its results
Explain how global budgets change hospital incentives around volume and prevention

content_blocks.body:
In fee-for-service, hospitals earn revenue when patients are admitted. They lose revenue when patients avoid hospitalization — through better primary care, prevention, or care management. Global budgets fundamentally change this: a hospital receives a fixed annual budget regardless of how many patients it admits. If it can keep patients healthy and out of the hospital, it keeps the budget. If volume rises above target, it must absorb the additional cost.

This is the most complete form of hospital payment reform — aligning hospital financial incentives with population health for the first time.
content_blocks.heading: The hospital volume problem

content_blocks.body:
Maryland has had a unique hospital payment system since 1977. The Health Services Cost Review Commission (HSCRC) sets hospital rates for all payers — Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial — under a federal waiver. In 2014, Maryland moved its hospitals to all-payer global budgets under the Maryland All-Payer Model, which ran from 2014 through 2018; in 2019 it entered the Total Cost of Care Model, adding a population-level global budget for Medicare spending across all care settings.

Results after 5 years: the independent evaluation (RTI International, 2019) found $975 million in Medicare savings from 2014 to 2018 — total Medicare spending grew 2.8 percent more slowly than in a comparison group, with $796 million of the savings from hospital spending. The federal AHEAD Model, which builds partly on Maryland's approach, began performance in Maryland in 2026, with Connecticut, Hawaii, Rhode Island and downstate New York slated to follow; Vermont signed on in January 2025 but withdrew in July 2026, and its hospital global budgets now proceed under state law (Act 68 of 2025).
